label: PART V
title: Modeling Systems That Can Change
lead: Place business rules and technology dependencies behind boundaries that match ownership and language.

chapters.title: Domain modeling and architectural boundaries
chapters.intro: Senior design is largely the work of placing rules, data, and dependencies behind boundaries that match the business. These concepts extend the object-level catalog into application-scale structure.

concepts.title: Domain Modeling
concepts.definition: Domain modeling represents business concepts, decisions, invariants, and transitions directly in code. Entities carry identity, value objects express meaning by value, and services hold rules that belong to no single object.
concepts.look_for: Start where a real business rule can be enforced at the moment state changes instead of leaving records valid only by convention.
concepts.walkthrough: `Order.Add` accepts the language of the business - a `Product` and a `quantity` - and prevents a nonpositive quantity from entering `_lines`. The caller cannot replace the line collection directly because `Lines` exposes a read-only view. `CalculateTotal` derives a meaningful order value from `OrderLine.UnitPrice` and `Quantity`; it does not make a controller or database row own that rule. This is domain modeling because code boundaries follow business responsibility and protect valid transitions, not because the class has the name `Order`. The shorthand versions compress the total calculation with LINQ or a generator expression after the explicit loop establishes the data flow. The lambda passed to `Sum` maps each line to its extended price and captures no outside state. A rich model earns its keep where rules interact and evolve; a simple record plus straightforward application code may be better for pure CRUD.
concepts.caution: Do not turn every database table into a ceremonious domain object. Invest in modeling where language, invariants, and change pressure are real, and keep persistence concerns from dictating the model unnecessarily.
concepts.related: Entity; Value Object; Domain Service; Aggregate

concepts.title: Ubiquitous Language and Bounded Context
concepts.definition: Ubiquitous Language uses domain experts' terms consistently in conversation and code. A bounded context defines where one model and vocabulary apply, allowing the same word to mean something different elsewhere.
concepts.look_for: Draw a boundary where terminology, rules, data ownership, or change cadence diverges, then translate explicitly rather than forcing one enterprise-wide model.
concepts.walkthrough: Sales uses `Customer` to reason about `CreditLimit`; Support uses `Customer` to reason about `SupportTier`. The shared human being does not require one shared software object because the two contexts answer different questions and evolve under different rules. Their namespaces make those meanings explicit. `Translate` crosses the boundary intentionally, carrying the stable customer identity and choosing a support-specific tier rather than leaking the sales model into Support. In Domain-Driven Design terms, the vocabulary within each context is ubiquitous when developers and domain experts use the same words with the same meanings. The boundary prevents one overloaded mega-model from accumulating every department's fields and constraints. Translation has a visible cost, but it localizes semantic change. A bounded context is a model boundary, not automatically a process, repository, team, or microservice; deployment boundaries may align with it when operational evidence supports that choice.
concepts.caution: Do not split contexts merely to permit duplicate class names, and do not erase genuine distinctions to avoid mapping code. Validate boundaries with domain experts and ownership, not folder aesthetics.
concepts.related: Domain-Driven Design; Context Map; Anti-Corruption Layer

concepts.title: Aggregate and Invariant Boundary
concepts.definition: An aggregate is the smallest cluster of domain state that must change consistently as one unit. Its root controls mutations and protects invariants; references to other aggregates normally use identity.
concepts.look_for: Choose the boundary around rules that must be true immediately after a command. Coordinate rules that can tolerate delay through events, commands, or reconciliation.
concepts.walkthrough: `Order` is the aggregate root: callers request `AddLine` and `Place` instead of mutating `_lines` or `Status`. `AddLine` prevents edits after placement, and `Place` checks both nonemptiness and the current lifecycle state before changing `Status`. Those checks make the invariant boundary concrete; after either method returns, the order remains valid according to the rules shown. `OrderLine` lives inside that consistency boundary, while `ProductId` points to a separate product aggregate by identity rather than embedding a mutable `Product` graph. An aggregate is therefore not simply any collection of objects and not necessarily one database transaction spanning the enterprise. It should be as small as the immediately consistent rules permit. Cross-aggregate workflows usually accept temporal separation and handle failure explicitly, which improves concurrency but requires business decisions about eventual consistency.
concepts.caution: Oversized aggregates cause contention, large loads, and unnecessary transaction conflicts. Undersized aggregates leak invariants into services. Base the boundary on consistency rules and concurrency, not object containment alone.
concepts.related: Entity; Invariant; Unit of Work; Domain Event

concepts.title: Architectural Boundaries and the Dependency Rule
concepts.definition: The dependency rule makes source-code dependencies point toward stable business policy. UI, database, network, and framework details depend on application or domain contracts rather than forcing core policy to depend on them.
concepts.look_for: A useful boundary lets core rules run in a plain test without starting a web host, database, message broker, or UI framework.
concepts.python_expanded:
from typing import Protocol


class PaymentGateway(Protocol):
    async def charge(self, amount):
        ...


class CheckoutService:
    def __init__(self, payments: PaymentGateway):
        self._payments = payments

    async def pay(self, order):
        amount = order.total
        result = await self._payments.charge(amount)
        return result


class StripePaymentGateway:
    async def charge(self, amount):
        result = await stripe_client.charge(amount)
        return result
concepts.walkthrough: `CheckoutService` depends on `IPaymentGateway`, a capability phrased in application terms. The concrete `StripePaymentGateway` depends inward by implementing that contract and translates to a vendor client. As a result, Stripe can be replaced and checkout policy can be tested with a fake gateway without making the application layer import vendor infrastructure. Dependency injection is the construction mechanism that supplies `_payments`; dependency inversion is the design principle that makes the high-level policy own or depend on the abstraction. Layered folders alone do not create this boundary - project references and imports must prevent core code from reaching outward. The goal is not that every dependency points to the domain, but that volatile details do not dictate stable policy. Data-only types may cross boundaries when deliberate; framework request objects and ORM entities usually should not become the domain's vocabulary.
concepts.caution: Interfaces added around every class create indirection without protecting a meaningful boundary. Place abstractions where volatility, ownership, testability, or policy direction justifies them, and enforce the rule mechanically.
concepts.related: Dependency Inversion Principle; Ports and Adapters; Clean Architecture

concepts.title: Ports and Adapters
concepts.definition: Ports and Adapters has the application define capability-oriented entry and exit ports while adapters translate those ports to technologies such as HTTP, SQL, files, queues, GUIs, and CLIs.
concepts.look_for: Introduce a port at a volatile or externally controlled edge when the application needs a stable vocabulary distinct from the technology's API.
concepts.walkthrough: `IOrderStore` is an output port: it states what the application needs in terms of orders, not connections, tables, or vendor exceptions. `SqlOrderStore` is an adapter because it implements that port by querying rows and translating them with `MapToDomain`. An HTTP controller or desktop view model could likewise be an input adapter that turns an external request into an application command. Business code can therefore run against the port while adapters absorb technical change at the edges. This architecture is also called Hexagonal Architecture. It is closely related to the dependency rule: the inner application owns the port, and the outer adapter depends inward on it. The interface should not merely photocopy every method of a database or SDK; it should capture an application capability at a boundary worth protecting. Python's `Protocol` makes the expected shape explicit while retaining structural typing.
concepts.caution: A one-for-one wrapper around every library creates pass-through layers without semantic value. Keep adapters thin, but let ports speak application language and translate errors, data, and lifecycle deliberately.

concepts.title: Modular Monolith Before Microservices
concepts.definition: A modular monolith deploys as one application while keeping business modules isolated through explicit contracts and data ownership. It preserves simple operations and leaves credible seams for later separation.
concepts.look_for: Prefer one deployable by default; split a module only when independent scale, release cadence, fault isolation, security, or ownership clearly outweighs distributed-system cost.
concepts.csharp_shorthand: public sealed record OrderPlaced(Guid OrderId, decimal Total);
concepts.walkthrough: Orders publishes the intentionally small `OrderPlaced` contract. `BillingOrderPlacedHandler` consumes that contract and writes through its own `IInvoiceStore`; it does not import Orders internals or query an Orders-owned table. The two modules can still communicate in memory and ship in one process, avoiding network calls, distributed tracing, service discovery, and cross-service deployment coordination. The boundary is nevertheless real because contracts and data ownership constrain dependencies. If Billing later needs independent deployment for scale or release cadence, `OrderPlaced` is a plausible seam for a broker adapter. This is not a promise that every module should become a service. The phrase 'before microservices' encodes a decision rule: earn distribution with evidence. A folder named `Billing` is insufficient if any code can reach into its schema or internal types; architecture tests and project/module visibility make the isolation credible.
concepts.caution: A monolith with shared tables and unrestricted imports is not modular. Conversely, premature asynchronous messaging inside one process can add distributed complexity before it buys any operational independence.

concepts.title: Repository, Unit of Work, and Persistence Ignorance
concepts.definition: A repository retrieves and stores aggregates in domain terms; a unit of work commits a coherent set of persistence changes atomically. Persistence ignorance keeps domain policy free of storage APIs and ORM lifecycle details.
concepts.look_for: Use these boundaries when domain operations should not know SQL or change tracking. Skip ceremonial wrappers when direct ORM access already expresses a simple data-access use case well.
concepts.python_expanded:
async with unit_of_work_factory.begin() as work:
    loaded_order = await order_repository.load(order_id)
    if loaded_order is None:
        raise OrderNotFound(order_id)

    loaded_order.place()
    await order_repository.save(loaded_order)
    await work.commit()
concepts.walkthrough: `orderRepository.LoadAsync` speaks in terms of an `Order` aggregate and its identifier, while `loadedOrder.Place` applies the domain transition without seeing SQL, ORM sessions, or entity states. `SaveAsync` registers the changed aggregate, and `work.CommitAsync` defines the atomic persistence boundary. The repository owns collection-like access to orders; the unit of work owns transaction and commit semantics. Many ORMs already implement both ideas internally, so adding `IGenericRepository<T>` over every table may only rename `Add`, `Update`, and `Delete`. A useful repository exposes domain-shaped queries and aggregate boundaries, not arbitrary table access. Persistence ignorance is a direction of dependency rather than a claim that storage never influences design: concurrency tokens, transaction size, and query needs still matter, but domain objects should not require an active database session to enforce their rules.
concepts.caution: Generic CRUD repositories often erase domain vocabulary and hide useful ORM capabilities. Define transaction ownership clearly, avoid lazy-loading surprises, and keep one unit of work from spanning unrelated long-running operations.

concepts.title: CQRS and Event Sourcing
concepts.definition: CQRS separates models for changing state and reading state when their needs diverge. Event sourcing stores an append-only history of domain events as the source of truth and rebuilds state by replay; either technique can be used without the other.
concepts.look_for: Use CQRS for materially different read and write concerns. Consider event sourcing only when historical truth, temporal queries, auditability, or event-driven behavior justify replay and versioning complexity.
concepts.python_expanded:
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PlaceOrderCommand:
    order_id: UUID


async def handle_place_order(command):
    await order_writer.place(command.order_id)


async def get_order_summary(order_id):
    summary = await order_reader.get_summary(order_id)
    return summary


# In an event-sourced write model, this fact becomes source data.
event = OrderPlaced(order_id, clock.utcnow())
await event_store.append(order_id, event, expected_version)
concepts.walkthrough: `HandleAsync` sends `PlaceOrderCommand` through `orderWriter`, while `GetSummaryAsync` reads a purpose-built `OrderSummary` through `orderReader`. That separation is CQRS: writes enforce state transitions and reads serve query shapes without requiring one shared model. The final `AppendAsync` line shows a separate decision, event sourcing, in which `OrderPlaced` is durable source data and `expectedVersion` supplies optimistic concurrency. A CQRS system may still store current rows, and an event-sourced aggregate may use the same model for reads and writes. Keeping the terms separate prevents accidental architecture inflation. Event sourcing adds event-schema evolution, replay, snapshotting, projection lag, and operational recovery. It is valuable when the sequence of facts is itself a business asset, not merely because publishing events sounds modern. Read models may be eventually consistent, so user workflows need an explicit freshness story.
concepts.caution: Both techniques multiply models and debugging paths. Do not adopt them for ordinary CRUD, and never treat events as immutable without a plan for privacy obligations, bad historical data, and version evolution.
